extracted.intended_audience: students, lawyers, researchers, and the general public interested in U.S. administrative law and federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards about how federal regulations are promulgated, published, and codified (the notice-and-comment rulemaking process, statutory and executive requirements, and CFR publication/citation conventions). Useful for understanding or preparing rulemakings and comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorizing statute components
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorizing statutes typically have two parts: (1) a substantive scope, typically using language such as "The Secretary shall promulgate regulations to [accomplish some purpose or within some scope]"; and (2) procedural requirements, typically to invoke rulemaking requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA), Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA), and several executive orders (primarily Executive Order 12866).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or drafting a regulation, confirm the enabling statute both defines the scope of regulatory authority and incorporates or triggers procedural obligations (e.g., APA NPRM/comment, PRA information-collection review, RFA small-entity analysis, EO 12866 review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) rulemaking requirements (5 U.S.C. §553)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA generally requires a process that includes publication of the proposed rules in a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM), certain analyses, a request for public comment and participation in the decision-making, and adoption and publication of the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key APA elements to satisfy: issue an NPRM with sufficient notice of proposed changes; provide opportunity for public comment; consider comments in the agency's decision; publish the final rule with required statement of basis and purpose. (The page cites 5 U.S.C. §553 as the relevant provision.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking that involves information collection must comply with the Paperwork Reduction Act (codified at 44 U.S.C. §§3501–3521).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must obtain OMB approval for new information collections, estimate and justify respondent burden, and follow PRA procedural requirements before finalizing rules that impose reporting/recordkeeping obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking must account for impacts on small entities as required by the Regulatory Flexibility Act (codified at 5 U.S.C. §§601–612).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should prepare initial and final regulatory flexibility analyses (or certify that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities) and consider alternatives to minimize small-entity impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12866 and cost–benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain executive orders (primarily Executive Order 12866) require agencies to perform cost–benefit or other regulatory review for covered rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For economically significant rules subject to EO 12866, prepare regulatory impact analyses, quantify benefits and costs where feasible, and submit required reviews to OMB (or otherwise follow the executive order's review procedures). The page refers to cost–benefit analyses in this context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication first in the Federal Register (NPRM and final rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules and regulations are first promulgated or published in the Federal Register; generally the process includes publication of the proposed rules in an NPRM and publication of the final rule in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must use the Federal Register for official notice: publish NPRMs to solicit comment and publish final rules (with effective dates and statement of basis/purpose). Compliance with Federal Register publication is a gateway to codification in the CFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment and participation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking procedures require a request for public comment and participation in the decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a meaningful opportunity for comment (adequate notice, sufficient factual/legal detail), consider and respond to significant comments in the rulemaking record, and ensure the record supports the agency's final determinations (important for judicial review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation of rulemaking authority (Parallel Table of Authorities and Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Parallel Table of Authorities and Rules lists rulemaking authority for regulations codified in the CFR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or evaluating regulations, include clear citations to the authorizing statute(s); codifiers and users rely on the Parallel Table to trace statutory authority for CFR provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFR structure and citation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFR is structured into 50 titles that are broken down into chapters, parts, sections and paragraphs. Example citation: "42 C.F.R. § 260.11(a)(1)" indicates title 42, part 260, section 11, paragraph (a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft regulatory text with the CFR codification structure in mind (part/section/paragraph divisions) and use standard citation formats to ensure proper placement and retrieval in the CFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: eCFR online updating practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to the annual printed edition, the CFR is published online on the Electronic CFR (eCFR) website, which is updated daily; the Office of the Federal Register keeps an unofficial online version normally updated within two days after changes published in the Federal Register become effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the eCFR for near-real-time access to current regulatory text; anticipate that published Federal Register changes will be reflected in the eCFR within about two days.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFR annual edition publication schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The printed volumes of the CFR are issued once each calendar year on a staggered schedule: Titles 1–16 updated as of January 1; Titles 17–27 as of April 1; Titles 28–41 as of July 1; Titles 42–50 as of October 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For citation to the annual edition or when relying on printed volumes, use the appropriate title-quarter update schedule; understand that the printed annual edition may lag behind daily eCFR updates.
